lead: A wing skin in the sun, a fuselage frame beside a hot bleed-air duct and a supersonic skin heated by the airflow all carry temperatures that change across the section. Material that is hotter wants to be longer. If the free thermal strain fits a plane section, the beam simply bends or stretches and no stress arises; whatever does not fit, or whatever the supports prevent, becomes stress. This chapter turns a temperature field into a free curvature and into thermal stresses, for a solid spar and for a boom section. Only a few universities teach it.
prereq: You need: plane sections and curvature from symmetrical bending, and the general formula of unsymmetrical bending.

sections.h3: Free thermal strain and free curvature

blocks.text: A temperature rise T (K) gives a free strain α T, where α is the coefficient of thermal expansion (about 23 × 10⁻⁶ per K for aluminium, 12 × 10⁻⁶ per K for steel). If T varies linearly through the depth h, the free strain is linear too, which is exactly what a plane section can follow. The beam bends with no stress at all:

blocks.where: R<sub>T</sub> is the free thermal radius of curvature (m); h is the depth (m); T<sub>top</sub> and T<sub>bot</sub> are the face temperatures (K or °C, only the difference matters). The hot face becomes convex.

blocks.text: In general the actual strain ε is plane, ε = ε₀ + y/R (plus an x term), and the stress is σ = E(ε − α T). The beam settles where the stresses give the external force and moments. Two cases are common:

items: Curvature prevented, axial extension free (a spar held straight by its supports): ε₀ is the mean of α T, and σ = E α (Tmean − T). For a linear field the faces carry ±E α ΔT/2, the hot face in compression. These stresses have zero net force but a net moment, which the supports must supply.

Free beam, non-linear field: the beam takes up the best-fitting plane strain, and only the part of α T that is not linear in x and y becomes stress. This stress has zero net force and zero net moments: it is self-equilibrating.

blocks.text: For a boom section the free case has a neat recipe. Work out the thermal force and moments, then subtract the free strain the boom cannot have:

N<sub>T</sub> = Σ E α T<sub>i</sub> A<sub>i</sub>,  M<sub>xT</sub> = Σ E α T<sub>i</sub> A<sub>i</sub> y<sub>i</sub>,  M<sub>yT</sub> = Σ E α T<sub>i</sub> A<sub>i</sub> x<sub>i</sub>;  σ<sub>i</sub> = −E α T<sub>i</sub> + N<sub>T</sub>/A + (general formula with M<sub>xT</sub>, M<sub>yT</sub>)
blocks.where: T<sub>i</sub> is the temperature rise of boom i, A<sub>i</sub> its area and (x<sub>i</sub>, y<sub>i</sub>) its position from the centroid; A is the total boom area. With I<sub>xy</sub> = 0 the last term is M<sub>xT</sub> y<sub>i</sub>/I<sub>xx</sub> + M<sub>yT</sub> x<sub>i</sub>/I<sub>yy</sub>.

spec.aria: Two small plots share the depth of a 100 millimetre spar. The first shows temperature falling linearly from 35 degrees at the top to 5 degrees at the bottom. The second shows stress: minus 24.15 megapascals compression at the top, zero at mid-depth, plus 24.15 tension at the bottom. On the right, a rectangle with four booms: boom 1 top right is heated and carries minus 20.1, boom 2 top left plus 20.1, boom 3 bottom left minus 20.1, boom 4 bottom right plus 20.1 megapascals. A note says the net force and both moments are zero.

examples.question: An aluminium spar is 100 mm deep, E = 70 GPa, α = 23 × 10⁻⁶ per K. The top flange is at 35 °C and the bottom flange at 5 °C, with a linear variation between. Find (a) the free radius and (b) the face stresses if the supports hold the spar straight but leave it free to extend.
steps: (a) 1/R<sub>T</sub> = α ΔT/h = 23 × 10⁻⁶ × 30/0.100 = 6.90 × 10⁻³ per m, so R<sub>T</sub> = 145 m. The hot top becomes convex: the spar bows upwards.
(b) The mean temperature is 20 °C, so the faces are 15 K above and below the mean.
Top (hot) face: −24.15 MPa, compression. Bottom (cool) face: +24.15 MPa, tension. The supports supply the moment E α (ΔT/h) I that holds the spar straight.
examples.answer: R<sub>T</sub> = 145 m when free; held straight, the faces carry −24.15 MPa (hot top) and +24.15 MPa (cool bottom).

examples.question: A free beam has four equal booms A at (±200, ±75) mm, E = 70 GPa, α = 23 × 10⁻⁶ per K. Boom 1 at (200, 75), next to a hot duct, warms by 50 K; the others stay cold. Find the boom stresses.
steps: E α T₁ = 70,000 × 23 × 10⁻⁶ × 50 = 80.5 N/mm². Call it s, so N<sub>T</sub> = s A, M<sub>xT</sub> = s A × 75 and M<sub>yT</sub> = s A × 200.
Section: total area 4A, I<sub>xx</sub> = 4A × 75², I<sub>yy</sub> = 4A × 200², I<sub>xy</sub> = 0.
Terms at boom i: N<sub>T</sub>/4A = s/4; M<sub>xT</sub> y<sub>i</sub>/I<sub>xx</sub> = s y<sub>i</sub>/(4 × 75); M<sub>yT</sub> x<sub>i</sub>/I<sub>yy</sub> = s x<sub>i</sub>/(4 × 200).
Checks: the four stresses sum to zero (no force), and Σσ y and Σσ x are both zero (no moments): the stress is self-equilibrating.
examples.answer: ±20.1 MPa in a chequer pattern: the heated boom and the boom diagonally opposite in compression, the other two in tension. The beam also bends and stretches freely.

traps: Using σ = E α ΔT on a free beam with a linear gradient. A free beam bows stress-free.
Forgetting the factor 1/2: a spar held straight carries ±E α ΔT/2 at its faces, not E α ΔT.
Calling the held-straight stress self-equilibrating. Its net force is zero but its net moment is not; the supports supply it.
Putting h in mm when the curvature is wanted per metre.
Leaving out the −E α T<sub>i</sub> term in a boom section; the formula then gives the thermal "moment stress" only.

quiz.q: Write the free thermal curvature of a beam with a linear temperature difference across its depth.
quiz.a: 1/R<sub>T</sub> = α(T<sub>top</sub> − T<sub>bot</sub>)/h; the hotter face becomes convex and no stress arises.

quiz.q: Why is a free beam with a linear temperature gradient stress-free?
quiz.a: Its free thermal strain is linear in y, which is a plane-section strain. The beam follows it exactly by bending and stretching, so the mechanical strain is zero everywhere.

quiz.q: An aluminium spar 80 mm deep, E = 72 GPa, α = 23 × 10⁻⁶ per K, has its top at 40 °C and bottom at 10 °C. Find the free radius, and the face stresses if it is held straight but free to extend.
quiz.a: 1/R<sub>T</sub> = 23 × 10⁻⁶ × 30/0.080 = 8.625 × 10⁻³ per m, R<sub>T</sub> = 115.9 m. Faces: ±72 × 10⁹ × 23 × 10⁻⁶ × 15 = ±24.84 MPa, the hot top in compression.

quiz.q: A steel spar (E = 200 GPa, α = 12 × 10⁻⁶ per K) with a 40 K top-to-bottom difference is held straight but free to extend. Find the face stress.
quiz.a: σ = ±E α ΔT/2 = 200 × 10⁹ × 12 × 10⁻⁶ × 20 = ±48 MPa, the hot face in compression.

quiz.q: A spar is held straight and also held against axial extension, with a uniform rise of 25 K. Find the stress for aluminium (E = 70 GPa, α = 23 × 10⁻⁶ per K).
quiz.a: Nothing can move, so σ = −E α T = −70 × 10⁹ × 23 × 10⁻⁶ × 25 = −40.25 MPa, uniform compression.

quiz.q: In the four-boom example, why is boom 3, which stays cold, in compression?
quiz.a: The heated boom makes the beam stretch and bend about both axes. The plane strain the section takes up is +3/4, +1/4, −1/4 and +1/4 of α T₁ at booms 1 to 4. Boom 3 is shortened although it is cold, so it is in compression; booms 2 and 4 are stretched although cold, so they are in tension; boom 1 is stretched less than it wants, so it is in compression too.

beyond: Composite skins have plies with different α, so a laminate cools from its cure temperature with built-in stress and can warp. Hypersonic vehicles see transient gradients large enough to cause thermal buckling of skin panels. Search for "thermal stress laminated plate" and "thermal buckling of panels".
